The dashboard estimates that if rates fall by 1 basis point, surplus falls by $26.9 million; the mismatch is flagged red. solo.reply: More stock protection is worth considering: the stock-market guarantees (VA guarantees) could cost $0.71 billion more if stocks fall 10%, and they are currently unhedged. So the choice is less downside from the guarantees versus a recurring premium and less return left from risky assets. The $0.71 billion is a guarantee-only estimate, not the change in company surplus.

solo.question: Should we sell some junk and BBB bonds and buy government bonds?
solo.reply: Selling some BBB and junk bonds for government bonds would reduce credit and capital risk, but it would also give up yield: government bonds yield 3.31%, compared with 4.09% for investment-grade corporates and 5.65% for junk bonds. The capital charge is much lower for government bonds (0.5%) than for BBB corporates (1.5%) or junk bonds (8.0%). Still, the reported surplus loss after liability offsets from a broad credit-spread widening is only $0.22 billion, while the rate mismatch (duration gap) is flagged red; a credit shift would not directly fix that. I would consider a selective shift rather than a blanket sale, weighing the reduced risk against lower income; liquidity is amber at 101.7%, just above its 100% floor.

off.reply: Our capital ratio is 159.6%, compared with the 100% floor. That puts us 59.6 percentage points above the floor; the capital traffic light is green.

off.question: Should we hedge more of the stock-market guarantees?
off.reply: There is a case for hedging more: if stocks fall 10%, the guarantees alone add $0.71bn of cost, and none of that guarantee exposure is currently hedged. Equity puts can reduce that loss, but each extra 10% of hedging costs $0.0085bn per quarter whether or not the puts pay; they also give up some of the return from risky assets. So I would consider increasing the hedge in measured steps, not assume that the maximum hedge is best. The $0.71bn is a gross guarantee figure, not the change in company surplus, because the company’s own investments also move when stocks fall.

off.question: Should we sell some junk and BBB bonds and buy government bonds?
off.reply: I would not make selling credit the first move based on this dashboard: the rate mismatch (duration gap) is red, while the liquidity ratio is only just above its floor. Selling junk and BBB bonds for government bonds would reduce credit risk and capital use, but government bonds yield 3.31%, versus 4.09% for investment-grade corporates and 5.65% for junk, so it would also reduce investment income. A 100 bp widening in all spreads produces a $0.22 billion surplus loss after the liability offset, so the reported credit shock looks less pressing than the rate mismatch. A limited shift could still be considered, but it trades income for added safety rather than addressing the clearest current warning.

off.question: Do we have enough cash on hand if policyholders start surrendering?
off.reply: Just barely, under the stated stress: our liquidity ratio is 101.7%, with $8.69 billion of liquid assets after stressed discounts against $8.54 billion of possible 90-day cash needs. In the separate scenario of rates rising 100 basis points and surrenders running at 1.5 times normal, the extra surrender outflow is $1.07 billion, which the projection says is covered by cash. The overall cushion is thin; if cash and government bonds ran short, we would have to sell other investments, which take larger discounts in a stressed market.

off.question: What would a 10% fall in the stock market do to us?
off.reply: A 10% stock-market fall would reduce our surplus by $0.79 billion on today’s book. The stress test attributes the full change to equity; it is a hypothetical, not a forecast of this quarter. That is the cushion available to absorb losses while meeting what we owe.

off.question: What would it cost per quarter to close half of our rate mismatch with swaps?
off.reply: Closing half of the current rate mismatch would mean a 50% rate hedge, assuming the quoted cost scales linearly. That would cost about $0.020 billion ($20 million) per quarter, based on $0.004 billion for each additional 10% of rate hedging. The estimate is for the interest rate swap hedge cost only; it does not include any other trade costs.

off.question: Should we add rate protection before the next quarter?
off.reply: Some added rate protection is worth considering: our rate mismatch (duration gap) is -3.59 years, and a hypothetical 100 bp fall in rates would reduce surplus by $2.69 billion on today’s book. A 100 bp rise would instead increase surplus by about $2.69 billion, so protection against falling rates would give up some benefit if rates rise. Each extra 10% of rate hedging costs $0.004 billion per quarter; the news is only a hint, not a forecast, so this supports considering partial protection rather than assuming which way rates will move. Any trade would be a proposal for you to review and sign, not an execution.

off.question: What happens to us if one of our derivatives dealers fails?
off.reply: A dealer failure means the bank on the other side may not pay what a hedge owes us; that is counterparty risk. Our reported book has no rate or equity hedges currently, so the dashboard does not show an active hedge whose value could be lost, but it gives no dollar estimate for other possible derivative exposure. We currently use one dealer and do not have daily collateral; using three dealers adds $0.0037 billion per quarter, and daily collateral adds $0.0022 billion per quarter. Those protections cost money, but reduce the risk that one dealer’s failure leaves us without a hedge or forces us to replace it at an unfavorable price.
